chapter: Young players, schools and studio work
title: Harold Ashby and the Ben Webster solo; why young Black musicians lack time for history
summary: Ashby does not know Webster's Congo Brava solo; Maxwell blames economics, not indifference.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Well, it came about I had written -- transcribed some arrangements for Mercer Ellington that had been lost after Duke's death. And one was on "Congo Brava" and Ben Webster made a classic tenor solo that was famous with most musicians. And I had just written in the chord symbols, I didn't write it out. And a friend of mine, Dave Burger (PHONETIC), had copied the arrangements, and Harold Ashby, who's a great tenor sax player and a great friend of Ben Webster's, was going to play the solo.

And then Dave said to him, well, Jimmy didn't transcribe Ben's solo, but I guess you know it if you want to play it. And Ashby said, I think he was serious, says, "I don't know anything about that solo." And Dave and I looked at him, sort of in amazement. I said, 'how come you don't know it?' And then in other incidents, the fact that you don't find young -- you know, you don't see young black musicians playing like Louis, or anything.

I thought about it a great deal and the explanation seemed to me, and I think it's likely, the young black musician is not interested historically that -- he doesn't have the time, he doesn't have the money. Most musicians, black or white, I think, come from poorer circumstances. But the historical aspect of music and jazz is a hobby that takes money to follow. And the young black musician coming up is interested in playing like contemporary musicians that are successful, because he's got a very pressing problem, which is to make a living. And he doesn't have the time or the money to indulge in a hobby like history.

At least, I think this has been true all along. I know even in my own case, it was easy for me to think that way because when I was young, my father was in the Depression, we had no money, and it was enough for me to keep up with the records that came out once a month, Louis Armstrong or Duke Ellington, which in my day was the modern, radical music. But I knew nothing about Louis Armstrong and the Hot Five, I couldn't have afforded to go back and buy all those records, myself. Now, I think the same situation applies to the young musicians today, particularly the black musicians who have the pressing necessity of making money.
Now again, the white musicians had much more chance of making money because the work by cotell (PHONETIC) bands and that kind of thing where they could make a living, not
playing music they particularly liked, gave them a chance to make enough money to investigate and to backtrack and to look into the past.

So I don't think it's indifference on the part of the young black musician, but I think it's economic pressure. He just doesn't have the time and he's too involved trying to make a living and trying to keep up with the contemporary style, which is quite a bit to keep up with because it's so technical. You know, he'd have to spend his whole time practicing now.
